speaker: The Announcer
text: Previously, on LAiDIES: our heroine learned that talking to AI isn't coding — it's delegation.

speaker: The Announcer
text: She stopped typing three vague words and hoping, and started briefing the machine like a smart new hire — David Rose specific — and got back something she'd actually send.

speaker: The Announcer
text: And on this episode: she gets an answer with full Regina George confidence, almost uses it... and then notices one tiny detail tugging at the corner of the story.

speaker: The Announcer
text: This is Episode Three: The Burn Book Problem.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a Thursday afternoon, and the machine just handed me something that looks glorious.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I'd asked one of the AI tools to turn four days of messy meeting notes into a clean client update.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Nine seconds later, there it was — structured, calm, completely sure of itself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It even opened with "per our discussion," which I would never, but somehow coming from the machine it read as competent instead of passive-aggressive.

speaker: The Heroine
text: I was two clicks from sending.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And then one sentence caught my eye.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The draft said the client had "approved" a July rollout.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Except — I was in that meeting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Nobody approved anything.

speaker: The Heroine
text: What we actually said was "July could work, if procurement clears by Friday." The machine took a maybe... and gave it a lanyard.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And I couldn't help but wonder... if a paragraph can sound that sure of itself — hair done, makeup done, "per our discussion" and everything — how am I supposed to catch the one line in it that's quietly, completely wrong.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Welcome back to LAiDIES — where smart, busy women learn AI one Wednesday at a time, from a little internet town called SUNNYVAiLE.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Last week, David Rose taught us to say what we actually want — fold in the cheese, but for your inbox.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This week, Elle Woods teaches us what to check before we believe what comes back.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Because here's what nobody warns you about when you start: AI can sound right.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And sounding right is not the same thing as being right.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Before your name goes on it, you need to know which kind of answer you're holding.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So I did what this town has taught me — I shut the laptop and took it to Main Street.

speaker: The Heroine
text: To the NewsStand on Main, whose job is separating what actually happened from what just sounds like it did.

speaker: The Heroine
text: No doom, no hype, no "a source close to the situation." And standing there with the real headlines, it landed: my draft didn't need a better writer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It needed someone at the news desk, holding every confident line up to the light — says who? based on what?

speaker: The Heroine
text: The machine had handed me a front page.

speaker: The Heroine
text: My job was to fact-check it before it ran under my byline.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Let me tell you about the Burn Book.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It didn't work because it was true — none of it was, and nobody checked.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It worked because it had social authority: a rumor, a grudge, a wild guess, and something fully unhinged, all in the same handwriting, with the same devastating teenage certainty.

speaker: The Heroine
text: AI writes in that same hand — that same certainty — but here's the twist: it doesn't only write rumors.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It'll take a real source, an old source, a similar-but-not-this source, and an assumption it made because the pattern looked familiar, and hand you one smooth paragraph like everyone in it belongs together.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's the Burn Book Problem: an official court record and an entry in the Burn Book come out in that exact same handwriting — same confidence, same finish — you can't tell which is which until you check.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Take the Bethany Byrd moment from Mean Girls — a perfect, tiny sourcing disaster.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Somebody ( Regina) writes in the Burn Book that Bethany must be lying about being a virgin — because she buys super-jumbo tampons.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One box of tampons, and boom — a verdict, filed.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Then the actual explanation walks in, much less scandalous and much more specific: she's just got a heavy flow and a wide set.....well you know the rest...

speaker: The Heroine
text: That was never evidence.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a clue in a Claire's headband, sprinting straight to a conclusion.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One data point.

speaker: The Heroine
text: No context.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Enormous conclusion.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So the question is never "can I use AI?" Yes.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Use it.

speaker: The Heroine
text: We are not here to churn butter by candlelight.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The question is: which parts is it just drafting for you — and which parts are claims that need receipts before they borrow your name?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now, a few wrong answers are easy to spot — the product that doesn't exist, the answer that argues with itself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But the fake citation?

speaker: The Heroine
text: That one's dressed to pass.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It looks exactly like a real source — cited with the confidence of "my boyfriend goes to another school" — right up until you click it and it goes nowhere.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the sneakiest one isn't fake at all.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's real information in the wrong place.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It brought the wrong ID and somehow made it past the door.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A U.S.

speaker: The Heroine
text: HR answer in a Canadian workplace.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Last year's pricing page wearing this year's lip gloss.

speaker: The Heroine
text: "We talked about it" quietly promoted to "we decided." A policy answer that's technically true, except the exception is the part that matters.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's the moment you stand up in the back, in your blue hoodie, strings pulled tight, and your oversized sunglasses, and you shout: "SHE DOESN'T EVEN GO HERE!"

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's not just a great line.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's a quality-control standard.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And this is where Elle Woods becomes the patron saint of AI verification.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Not because she makes "being thorough" sound corporate — because she spots the one detail everyone else treated like lip gloss and realizes it's holding up the alibi.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Chutney says she was in the shower, right after getting a perm.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Elle asks again.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Chutney gives the same story.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The room rolls its eyes, because it sounds like Elle is making haircare small talk in the middle of a murder trial.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But Elle isn't checking whether Chutney can repeat herself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: She's waiting for the detail that doesn't fit.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if you know one thing about perms, you know you do not wash a fresh one — not unless you're trying to destroy your alibi and your hair in the same afternoon.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One tiny beauty-world rule nobody took seriously... and the story falls apart.

speaker: The Heroine
text: With AI, that's the job.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Don't ask "does this sound smart?" Chutney sounded smart.

speaker: The Heroine
text: She sounded smart three times.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Ask: what's the one detail that can't survive contact with the timeline?

speaker: The Heroine
text: If it says a policy changed — what date proves it?

speaker: The Heroine
text: If it says a quote came from a person — where's the quote?

speaker: The Heroine
text: If it says a number went up — from what, over what timeframe, according to whom?

speaker: The Heroine
text: Do not be Chutney on the stand.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Be Elle with the timeline.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So before an answer leaves your laptop, sort it into three piles.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A draft is wording, structure, a brainstorm, a summary — that can be fast.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A claim is a name, a date, a number, a quote, a source, anything legal, HR, privacy, or money — that needs checking.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And a receipt is the thing you can actually open, name, or point to if someone asks.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A draft is an outfit.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A claim is an alibi.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Dress accordingly.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And before this sounds like a second job — remember who you are here.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You're Elle.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You're the one who stands up in that courtroom, finds the detail that doesn't hold up, and wins with her name on the case.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Nobody hands you that part.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But here's what Elle didn't have: a law clerk who already did the reading.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The machine spent the weekend in the library so you didn't — it did the research, it drafted the brief.

speaker: The Heroine
text: You still read it, you still check the citations, you still walk in and own it — because when the judge looks up, she's looking at you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's not extra work.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The grunt work got done for you; the judgment stayed yours.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And please — asking AI "are you sure?" is like asking Regina George whether the Burn Book is peer reviewed.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Bold choice.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Limited value.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Sometimes it catches the mistake, corrects itself, and we all briefly believe in personal growth.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And sometimes it just hands you the same wrong answer in the same questionable outfit consisting of two popped-collar polos, one over the other (of course), but this time with the shirt order switched.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's not verification.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's Chutney repeating the alibi in the same questionable outfit, just with a slightly different colour combo.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — before someone in the back adjusts a butterfly clip and says, "but the tools are getting better" — yes.

speaker: The Heroine
text: They are.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The newer ones can search, cite, read documents you hand them, and sometimes flag when they're unsure.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's real, and it helps.

speaker: The Heroine
text: But better is not solved.

speaker: The Heroine
text: A 2026 Nature paper put a name to why: the way we grade these models rewards a confident guess over an honest "I don't know" — so they guess.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Stanford's 2026 AI Index found something scarier for our purposes: tell a top model something false that you seem to believe, and it'll often just agree with you.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And KPMG — one of the Big Four accounting firms, the serious-suit people — had to pull an AI report after someone checked its sources and found forty of the forty-five were made up.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Forty of forty-five.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Big Four.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Tiny receipt drawer.

speaker: The Heroine
text: So attach the sources, absolutely.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Just don't assume "sources attached" means "sources checked." Sometimes it's still Chutney, handing you a folder in her own handwriting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the good news is, the serious guidance — from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Stanford — all points the same way, and it comes down to three moves.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Move one: give her the source.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Don't ask the machine what it remembers — paste the real document, the actual policy, this year's pricing page; when you need something current, turn on its search mode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Then one line: "answer only from what I just gave you." Elle doesn't argue from memory.

speaker: The Heroine
text: She walks in with the file.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Move two: let her say "I don't know." Add the sentence most people never think to add — "if it's not in there, say so; don't fill the gap." That one line is what turns a confident guess back into an honest blank.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Move three: make her show the line by asking:

speaker: The Heroine
text: "Quote the exact sentence you got that from."

speaker: The Heroine
text: If she can't point to it, that claim showed up at Spring Fling with no student ID — and it doesn't get to speak.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One rule over all three: no invented receipts.

speaker: The Heroine
text: No made-up links, dates, quotes, or numbers.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Watch it work on my Thursday disaster.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Instead of "clean up these notes," I pasted the notes and said: summarize only what's here, mark anything we didn't actually decide as "pending," and show me the line behind every claim.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Same nine seconds — no phantom July approval, because I never left a gap for the machine to fill.

speaker: The Heroine
text: That's Prompt Like Elle: hand her the file, let her say "I don't know," make her show the line.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Which brings me to my favourite part of every episode — the cocktail party explanation.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The answer you'll give the next time someone at happy hour puts down her drink and asks, "wait — why does it just make things up?" Here it is: it's not lying.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Lying takes intent.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's guessing.

speaker: The Heroine
text: When the machine doesn't know, it doesn't stop — it reaches for the most plausible-sounding thing and says it with its whole chest.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's your most confident friend.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The one who will answer any question, whether or not she actually knows.

speaker: The Heroine
text: The fix was never to catch her in a lie.

speaker: The Heroine
text: It's to ask for the receipt before you repeat her in a meeting.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And... that's the episode.

speaker: The Heroine
text: Now — your try-on.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And if you'd rather read than listen, the full episode's written up there too — every source laid out where you can check it yourself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the exact Prompt Like Elle wording — the three moves, copy-paste ready — is waiting in your try-on.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And the full rulebook — the three moves, the check patterns, all of it — is shelved in the library, to keep and pull down whenever an answer looks a little too sure of itself.

speaker: The Heroine
text: This week: take one real answer from an AI tool — a meeting recap, a summary of a public page, a draft reply — and verify three claims before it borrows your name.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One that leans on a name, a date, a number, or a link.

speaker: The Heroine
text: One that could be stale, or from the wrong country, or the wrong client.

speaker: The Heroine
text: And one you'd be embarrassed to say out loud if someone asked, "where did that come from?" You need ten minutes and enough self-respect not to let Chutney handle the timeline.
